summary.title: My Philosophy On Alerting
summary.one_liner: Learn how to design and audit alerting rules so pages are urgent, actionable and symptom-based, keeping on-call rotations quiet.
takeaways: Pages should be urgent, important, actionable and real, representing ongoing or imminent problems; remove noisy alerts rather than over-monitor.
Alert on user-visible symptoms (availability, latency, correctness, features) rather than individual causes, while using causes for dashboards and context.
Alert from the client or load balancer perspective where possible, since it reflects what users actually experience.
Route non-urgent problems to tickets, daily reports or workflow systems with clear accountability instead of paging.
Track pages and review alert accuracy regularly; alerts that are less than 50% accurate are broken.
summary.summary: This is a repost by Jack Neely of Rob Ewaschuk's essay on alerting, drawn from Ewaschuk's years of on-call work as an SRE at Google. It lays out a philosophy and a set of questions for writing or reviewing paging rules, arguing for symptom-based monitoring over cause-based alerts. It also covers handling sub-critical alerts through tickets and reports, writing playbooks, tracking alert accuracy, and exceptions where breaking these guidelines makes sense. The text is conceptual and includes an example of a terse multi-cause page summary, with no tools or code.
